title: Async Collaboration for Distributed Teams
summary: When your teammates are asleep while you work, every question costs a day. This is the mechanics — handoff design, overlap-hour budgeting, decision deadlines and lazy consensus — that keep a distributed team moving.

slides.markdown:
On a co-located team, a blocking question costs thirty seconds. Across a twelve-hour gap it costs a day — and a decision needing four exchanges costs a working week.

That single change in round-trip cost is what makes distributed collaboration a different discipline rather than the same one over video. Everything follows from it: work has to be handed off in a state someone else can pick up cold, decisions need deadlines instead of meetings, and the few overlapping hours have to be spent on things that genuinely require both people awake.

This topic is the **process** side of that — handoffs, overlap budgeting, decision mechanics, and when to break async and just get on a call. How to write the documents themselves is its own subject.

slides.subTitle: Sync and async aren't interchangeable
slides.markdown:
The two modes have different entry requirements, and most distributed-team friction is one being used where the other was needed.

**Synchronous** demands shared availability and shared attention. In exchange it gives you fast iteration, tone and body language, and immediate resolution of ambiguity. It leaves no artifact by default, and it excludes anyone who wasn't in the room.

**Asynchronous** demands *completeness*. A question that only half-specifies the situation gets a clarifying question back, and now you've spent a full day round trip on a misunderstanding. In exchange it's inclusive of every timezone, produces a record automatically, and lets people think before responding rather than perform an answer on the spot.

That completeness requirement is the skill people underestimate. "Can you look at the deploy issue?" is a fine sync question and a wasted day async. The async version is: what you saw, what you tried, the exact error, the two options you're weighing, and which one you'll take if you don't hear back.

A useful default for distributed teams: **async-first, sync by exception** — and be explicit about which exception you're invoking.

slides.subTitle: Why one exchange per day changes everything
slides.markdown:
Put real numbers on it. San Francisco and Bangalore are 12.5 hours apart, with roughly **zero natural overlap** in standard hours. Berlin and New York have about three hours. Sydney and London have essentially none.

On a zero-overlap pair, each exchange is one working day:

- Question asked Monday 5pm SF, read Tuesday 9am IST, answered, read Tuesday 9am SF.
- One clarifying question in that reply adds another full day.
- A four-exchange discussion takes the whole week.

The behavioral consequence is the point: **the number of round trips, not the amount of writing, is what determines how long anything takes.** So you optimize for fewer exchanges, even when that means writing much more per message.

Concretely, that flips several habits:

- Ask a question **with your proposed answer attached**, so the reply can be "yes" instead of "what do you think?"
- Send the whole review at once, never one comment at a time — a ping-pong review that costs hours co-located costs a week across a 12-hour gap.
- Pre-answer the obvious follow-ups. Three extra paragraphs beats one extra day.

A long message is cheap. A round trip is not.

slides.subTitle: Leave it pick-up-able
slides.markdown:
A handoff works when the next person can make progress **without asking you anything**. That's the bar, and it's higher than a status update.

What a usable end-of-day handoff contains:

- **State** — "branch `fix/checkout-timeout`, pushed, CI green, PR #421 open."
- **Where I stopped and why** — "reproduced the timeout locally; it's the retry loop, not the DB."
- **The next concrete step** — "needs the backoff jitter added in `RetryPolicy.next_delay`."
- **Anything blocking** — "needs a staging DB snapshot, I've requested it from platform."
- **Decisions you'd otherwise wait on, pre-decided** — "I'm assuming we cap retries at 3; say so if you disagree, otherwise I'll ship it."

That last line is the highest-leverage habit in distributed work. Every question you leave open costs the other person a day of waiting or a guess.

Two structural choices help more than discipline does. **Split work so ownership doesn't cross the gap** — follow-the-sun on a single ticket sounds efficient and mostly generates handoff overhead; parallel ownership of separate slices avoids the handoff entirely. And put the handoff **on the ticket or PR**, not in a DM, so anyone can pick it up if the intended person is out.

slides.subTitle: The scarcest resource on the team
slides.markdown:
If you share three hours a day, those hours are the most expensive real estate the team owns — and they get spent by default on status meetings, which is exactly what they're worst at.

Treat overlap as a budget with a spending rule: **only things that genuinely require both people awake at once.**

- **Worth overlap:** unblocking someone who's stuck, resolving a disagreement that's been through two async rounds, whiteboarding a design that isn't yet shaped, hard conversations, and deliberate relationship-building — which is not optional overhead on a distributed team.
- **Not worth overlap:** status updates (a written update is better and reaches everyone), demos (record them), routine code review, and anything one person can decide alone.

Practical moves that recover overlap hours:

- **Publish everyone's real working hours** in a shared calendar or a `TEAM.md`, and let people block focus time inside the overlap.
- **Rotate the pain.** If the only shared slot is 7am for one side and 8pm for the other, alternate who takes the bad end — permanently sacrificing one region's evenings is how you lose people from it.
- **Default meetings to 25 minutes** and require an agenda, because a shared hour is worth far more here than the calendar suggests.

With near-zero overlap, don't fake it — go fully async and accept a scheduled sync once a week or fortnight.

slides.subTitle: Proposal plus a deadline
slides.markdown:
The default decision procedure — get everyone in a room — doesn't survive a timezone spread, so distributed teams need a written one. The mechanic that works is a **proposal with a named decider and an explicit comment deadline**.

The structure of the announcement matters more than the length of the document:

> **Proposal:** move session storage from the app DB to Redis.
> **Decider:** me, as owner of the auth service.
> **Comment by:** Thursday 17:00 UTC.
> **If no objections by then**, I'll start the migration Friday.
> **Explicitly want input from:** @platform on the Redis cluster sizing.

Four things make this work, and skipping any one of them is where teams fail:

- **A single named decider**, not "the team." Shared ownership of a decision means nobody closes it.
- **A deadline with a timezone**, so it's unambiguous and creates real urgency.
- **A default action** stated up front — what happens if nobody replies.
- **Named individuals** whose input is actually required, so the people who must engage know they're not in the general audience.

The reason a deadline is essential rather than nice: without one, an async decision has no forcing function at all, and "we're still gathering feedback" is a state that can persist indefinitely.

slides.subTitle: Lazy consensus
slides.markdown:
Async decisions stall on an ambiguity: does no reply mean approval, or that nobody has read it yet? If silence means nothing, every decision needs explicit sign-off from everyone, and one person on holiday blocks the team.

**Lazy consensus** — the convention Apache projects have run on for decades — resolves it by declaring in advance that silence *is* consent after a stated window. No response by the deadline means go ahead.

It only works if three conditions hold, and they're the part teams skip:

- **The window is genuinely long enough** to cover every timezone and a normal amount of PTO. Two to three business days is the usual floor; 24 hours excludes people structurally.
- **It was actually visible** — posted where the affected people look, and tagged to individuals for anything high-impact, not dropped in a busy channel.
- **Objecting is cheap and safe.** "I need more time on this" must be a normal, respected response. If pushing back is socially expensive, silence stops meaning consent and starts meaning fear, and the convention is now laundering agreement that doesn't exist.

Scale the window to the blast radius: a config change can take a day, a schema migration or an API contract change deserves a week and an explicit ack from the affected owners rather than lazy consensus at all.

slides.sectionTitle: When the call is actually faster
slides.markdown:
Async-first is a default, not a religion. Some things are genuinely cheaper synchronously:

| | Stay async | Get on a call |
|---|---|---|
| **Situation** | a decision with clear options, a review, a status update | a design with no agreed shape yet, a stalled disagreement |
| **Signal** | each exchange moves the discussion forward | third round, same point, nobody's position has moved |
| **Emotional load** | neutral, technical | frustration is showing up in the thread |
| **Participants** | many, across timezones | two or three who need to converge |
| **Cost of the wrong choice** | a call that could have been a message | a five-day thread that a ten-minute call would end |

The reliable trigger is **the third round with no movement**. At that point text isn't slow — it's failing, because tone and nuance are being lost and each side is re-reading the other uncharitably.

Whatever the medium, the outcome has to land back in writing. A decision made on a call and never written down is invisible to everyone who wasn't on it and gets relitigated in six weeks. One paragraph on the ticket, posted by whoever called the meeting, is the whole obligation — and it's what keeps the sync exception from quietly eroding the async default.

Every review anti-pattern gets worse across a timezone gap, because each round trip is a day instead of an hour.

What changes concretely:

- **Review before your own work, not after.** Your reviewer's morning is your evening; a PR you review at 9am unblocks someone for their whole day, while one you get to at 5pm costs them a day.
- **Never drip comments.** Read the whole diff, batch every comment, submit once. Serial review costs hours co-located and a week at 12 hours apart — this is the single highest-cost habit across a gap.
- **Say what would satisfy you**, not just what's wrong. "Add a test for the empty-batch case and I'm happy" lets the author finish and merge; "needs more test coverage" costs a round trip just to find out what you meant.
- **Answer the question you think they'll ask next.** If you request a change, include the reason and the alternative you'd accept.
- **Never block and disappear.** If you can't come back within a day, leave the comment non-blocking, or hand the block to another owner explicitly.

Authors have a job too: open the PR **before** the end of your day, not after, and make the description carry everything a reviewer needs — they cannot tap you on the shoulder.

A team needs to choose a queueing technology. Someone says "let's discuss this in a meeting." Finding a slot across four timezones takes ten days. Two people can't make it, so it's rescheduled. Six weeks later, no decision, and three services have shipped inconsistent workarounds in the meantime.

The trap is that requiring a meeting **feels** responsible — it looks like taking the decision seriously. What it actually does is bind the decision to the scarcest resource the team has.

The symptoms are recognizable before six weeks pass:

- "We should sync on this" with no date attached.
- A decision that's been "almost made" through three separate conversations.
- People building workarounds because the decision hasn't landed.

The counter is to make the async path the default and the meeting the escalation: write the proposal, name the decider, set a deadline, and let the meeting be optional — scheduled *within* the comment window for whoever wants to talk, but not a precondition for deciding.

And give any stalled decision an owner with a date. Most stalls aren't disagreement; they're an unowned decision that everybody assumed someone else would close.

slides.subTitle: What happens in the room stays in the room
slides.markdown:
The subtler distributed-team failure isn't stalling — it's a **two-tier team**. The people who share an office or a timezone with leadership make decisions in hallway conversations, and everyone else finds out afterwards, as a fait accompli.

Nobody intends this. It's just faster to turn to the person next to you, and each individual instance is harmless. The cumulative effect is that remote members are structurally less influential, get less context, and are promoted less — which is a retention problem long before anyone names it.

The counters are mechanical:

- **Any decision made verbally gets written up**, by whoever was in the room, in the shared channel. Not a courtesy — a requirement.
- **If some participants are remote, everyone dials in individually.** A hybrid meeting with five people around one mic and two on a laptop is two meetings, and the remote one loses.
- **Record and transcribe** the meetings that must be sync, so people who were asleep can catch up.
- **Watch who's actually deciding things.** If every architectural call for six months came from the headquarters timezone, that's data, not coincidence.

The test worth applying periodically: could someone twelve hours away reconstruct why the last three significant decisions were made, from what's written down?

Distributed collaboration comes down to a handful of habits, all of them downstream of one fact: **a round trip costs a day, so minimize round trips, not keystrokes.**

- Ask questions with your proposed answer already attached.
- Hand off work in a state someone can pick up without asking you anything, and pre-decide the small calls you'd otherwise wait on.
- Give every decision a named decider, a deadline with a timezone, and a stated default if nobody replies.
- Make silence safe with a window long enough to cover PTO, and make objecting cheap.
- Spend overlap hours only on what needs both people awake, and rotate who takes the bad end of the clock.
- Break async when a thread hits its third round with no movement — then write the outcome back down.

The underlying principle is that **written and asynchronous is the more inclusive default**, and the discipline it demands — completeness, explicit deadlines, real decision ownership — tends to make co-located teams better too.

That closes this group: what review is for, how to give and take feedback, the process around it, the anti-patterns, real-time collaboration, and now collaboration across the clock.
